newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Blair set for showdown over pensions.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Blair set for showdown over pensions.

text.p: British opposition leader Tony Blair is getting an early taste of the trouble he can expect at his Labour party's annual conference next week from left-wingers unhappy at his safety-first strategy for regaining power.
With a general election now less than eight months away, Blair is hoping to use the conference in the northern resort of Blackpool to make Labour's 20-point poll lead unassailable.
But although Blair offers his party the prospect of power for the first time since 1979, the week-long gathering will be anything but a a sugar-coated send-off for the election.

Blair faces the real prospect of embarrassing defeats over workers' rights and pensions at the hands of activists eager to remind him that, despite his wooing of the middle classes, Labour's heart still beats on the left.

Pensions promises to be the most emotional issue because Baroness Barbara Castle, the grand old lady of Labour, has spearheaded a campaign to restore a link between the state pension and average earnings.
Pensions currently increase in line with inflation. Because prices rise more slowly than earnings, that means they shrink in value each year as a percentage of take-home pay.

Harriet Harman, the party's social security spokesman, says it would cost 3.5 billion pounds ($5.46 billion) to restore the earnings link for Britain's 10 million pensioners -- money that Labour, fearful of being tagged by the ruling Conservatives as taxers and spenders, says it cannot afford to find.
Harman wants instead to provide the 700,000 neediest pensioners with a top-up to their pension entitlement.
"It is right that the Labour party should have as its priority the poorest and it is wrong for the Labour Party if it is not sure that we can keep them," Harman said.
She and Blair have been lobbying the trade unions, which cast 50 percent of the votes at Labour's conference, to withhold their support for Castle in Wednesday's vote.

But Castle, 85, who established the link between pensions and earnings when she was a cabinet minister, accused Harman on Friday of "talking through her hat" and vowed to take her fight to the conference floor.

"I'm not a wrecker. Never have been, never will be. But I have a conscience and I couldn't die happy without putting up a fight for something which my whole history, 70 years in public life, tells me a civilised society should have," she told BBC television.
Castle said she of course wanted Blair to win the election but warned that his rush to capture the political middle ground could backfire.
"What's happening is that we're becoming more and more indistinguishable from the Tories. And if you think that's the way to win the election, I think it's a gross mis-estimate of what's happening.
"And remember, I've been through every general election since the war... I've seen the tactics fail," Castle said. ($1=.6405 Pound)
